disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more depressive episodes lasting at least two weeks, during which individuals experience a persistently low or irritable mood and/or markedly diminished interest or pleasure in most activities, accompanied by additional cognitive, physical, or emotional changes that cause significant distress or functional impairment. Typical features include alterations in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, self-worth, and thoughts about death or suicide, but the specific symptom pattern and severity can vary widely across individuals and episodes. The course may be single-episode or recurrent, often emerging in the context of psychosocial stressors but not fully explained by them, and it is distinguished from normal sadness by its pervasiveness, duration, and impact on functioning, as well as from bipolar disorders by the absence of past manic or hypomanic episodes. Accurate diagnosis requires ruling out substance-induced or medical causes and differentiating it from grief reactions and adjustment disorders that are more time-limited or stressor-bound.

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Luis’s consulting work with tech startups became increasingly unstable, with two major contracts ending abruptly and a third being scaled back, leaving him largely out of the workforce for the first time since his twenties. Initially he treated the gap as an opportunity to pour energy into his model railways, cycling, and woodworking, but as months passed without new projects and his savings projections began to look tighter than he had planned, he found it harder to justify his hobbies and more difficult to structure his days. About a month before presentation, after a promising lead on a long-term contract fell through at the final interview stage, he noticed himself spending long stretches sitting in his workshop without actually starting any projects, skipping his regular rides along Lake Michigan, and canceling on his small book club because "it didn’t seem worth the effort." His sister, alarmed by how unlike himself he sounded on the phone and by his admission that he hadn’t touched his trains or tools in weeks, urged him to contact his primary care physician, who referred him for a psychiatric evaluation when it became clear that his low motivation and disengagement were interfering with basic daily functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: I don’t get any enjoyment out of the things I used to love doing, and I can’t make myself start anything anymore.

narrative.stressor: Dora had prided herself on staying active in retirement—leading financial-literacy workshops, organizing events at the senior center, and hiking with the Senior Mountain Explorers. Six weeks before seeking help, she underwent an unexpected knee procedure after a fall on a local trail, which significantly limited her mobility and forced her to step back from gardening, dance nights, and her usual volunteer commitments. As she recovered at home in Colorado Springs, she found herself spending more time alone, brooding over her physical limitations and worrying that she might never return to her previous level of independence, and she began handing off leadership of her community programs to others. After a month of steadily pulling back from book club meetings and ignoring calls from mentees, one of her closest friends visited, noticed how uncharacteristically disengaged and self-critical she had become about "being a burden," and convinced her to talk with her primary doctor, who then referred her to psychiatry when it was clear her mood and outlook had shifted enough to disrupt her daily routines.
narrative.chief_complaint: I can’t shake this feeling that I’m useless now and just letting everyone down since my fall.

narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to his presentation, Robert had been pushing himself hard—working as a therapy assistant, leading teen groups, and taking on extra documentation responsibilities at the clinic while also staying up late to practice guitar and keep up with friends. About five weeks before seeking care, a cluster of difficult cases at work and a tense disagreement with a supervising clinician about treatment plans left him questioning his competence and worrying that he was "out of his depth" in mental health work. Over the following month, he became increasingly withdrawn after shifts, spending long nights alone in his apartment ruminating about whether his clients were getting worse because of him and scrolling through social media posts about burnout and failure in helping professions. When he began having intrusive thoughts about not wanting to wake up and drafted a note on his phone after a particularly stressful day at the clinic, he confided in a trusted colleague, who immediately alerted their supervisor and helped arrange an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I keep thinking my clients would be better off if I just weren’t here, and those thoughts about not wanting to wake up are starting to scare me.
